chapter_theme: Three songs at Thirukkutralam (திருக்குற்றாலம்): the courtesans who dance for money and pull the ladder away, the diseased body bound for Yama's town and hell, a plea for the Absolute beyond Veda and knowledge, and the poet who writes on women's breasts as poets write on palm leaf; the shrine is set above a list of famous temples and among devotees and siddhas.

975.reading: The poet names the courtesans who speak harm, dance for the coins thrown to them, lift a man up and then pull the ladder away, and the lustful men who sink with them, till wind diseases, colic and other ailments take the body and Yama, who never lets go of his noose, drags it to his town and a ruined hell; he asks Murugan to cut away this illusion and give his support. The praise sounds the battle in drum syllables, with ghosts gaping as Sura's armies die before the rider of the golden peacock, and sets Kutralam, thronged with faultless devotees, ascetics and siddhas, above Koodal, Siramalai, Kazhi, Karuvur and other shrines.
975.nuance: ஏறிட்டிட்டு ஏணியை வீழ்விடு முழுமாயர்: the women raise a man up and kick away the ladder, an image of the bargain's end. The song carries the courtesan's harm through to disease, Yama's noose and hell, one chain of consequence. The list of shrines in the praise ranks Kutralam above Madurai and the other famed centres.

976.reading: The poet asks to be given, as an honour, the life that is not learned in the Veda, not seen by understanding, has no distance in space, is hard for seekers of salvation to find, is not burned by fire or shaken by wind, the great light within fragrance, and far from those drunk with maya. The praise speaks obscurely of those who recite 'this is evil' yet never see the path, and names Murugan who, mad for the girl, took a hunter's form and came to live among the hunters, the lord of Kutralam among devotees, ascetics and siddhas.
976.nuance: The whole plea is a string of negations ending in -அது (கேள்வியிலாதது, காணவொணாதது, வேகாதது), the way the Upanishads speak of the Self as what fire does not burn nor wind dry; what is asked for is that state itself (வாழ்வை ... அருள்வாயே), not escape from women or death. The opening of the second half is hard to divide and the reading of it is a guess.

977.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander daily over breasts that bear nail-marks like palm leaves scored by poets of elaborate verse, captive to women whose eyes tear at their pearl ear-ornaments and fight like spears, and asks for grace to praise truly the golden lotus feet that the gods praise. The praise names Rama, who made the ten-headed king of demons give up his breath, and Siva, who cut off Brahma's extra head and broke the sun's teeth in anger, and ends at Kutralam where jackfruit, plantain and leaping fish fill the little river.
977.nuance: வித்தார கவித்திறத்தினர் பட்டோலை நிகர்த்து: the poet compares the scored breasts to a poet's written palm leaf, a craftsman's self-aware simile. பற்பாசன் மிகைச் சிரத்தை அறுத்து ஆதவனைச் சினத்துறு பல் போக உடைத்த: Siva cutting Brahma's fifth head and breaking the sun's teeth, the latter a detail of the destruction of Daksha's sacrifice.

links.note: 975 calls the courtesans those who raise a man up and let the ladder fall (ஏறிட்டிட்டு ஏணியை வீழ்விடு). Naladiyar 372 tells of the woman who swore to leap with him from the peak and, at the peak, having no gold from him, showed a pain in her feet and would not come (மேற்காணம் இன்மையான் மேவாது ஒழிந்தாள்). Both picture the bargain as a climb that she abandons at the top when the money ends.

976 asks for the life that is not heard in the Veda (வேதத்திற் கேள்வி யிலாதது) and not seen by understanding (போதத்திற் காண வொணாதது), naming it only by negations. Tirumular says the Veda and conduct end in kalanta and the great one is beyond speech, word and feeling (பேசா உரையுணர்வற்ற). Both describe the goal as what lies past the Veda and past the mind that knows.

977 compares women's nail-scored breasts to the written palm leaf of poets of elaborate verse (வித்தார கவித்திறத்தினர் பட்டோலை நிகர்த்து). 979 rehearses the stock comparisons of women's breasts and then confesses the base trade (இழிதொழில்) of making such praise-songs for patrons. The two songs show the poet's own craft turned on desire, first as a simile, then as the thing he wants to give up.
